title: How do you prepare for online tests like McKinsey Solve and BCG Casey?
description: What to expect from online assessments that some consulting firms use before interviews, such as problem-solving games and chat-based cases, and how to…
hook: Prepare for online tests like McKinsey Solve and BCG Casey by confirming the exact format in your invitation, practising the skills they all share (reading data quickly, business maths, and choosing what matters under time pressure), and doing any official practice the firm provides. They look different from a live case, but they test the same thinking. Here is what each common format involves as of 2026, and how to get ready without chasing outdated guides.
body:
The formats you might meet

Many firms add an online step before, or alongside, the first live interviews. Formats change by firm, office, role and year, so treat this as a map rather than a promise.

FormatWhat it involvesExample
Problem-solving gameScenario-based tasks in a game-like interfaceMcKinsey Solve
Chatbot caseA written case led by an automated interviewer, then a short videoBCG's online case, Casey
Aptitude testTimed numerical, verbal or logical questionsUsed by Bain and others in some offices
Recorded videoAnswers to fit or case questions with no live interviewerVarious firms
Written caseRead a pack of data, then prepare slides or a memo and presentUsually in later rounds; see group and written cases

McKinsey Solve

McKinsey describes Solve as a gamified assessment of natural problem-solving ability, used for most of its consulting roles, and says on its interviewing page that there is no need to prepare. In practice, being familiar with the format and comfortable with data still helps you stay calm.

As of 2026, candidates most often report two games: Redrock, a study in which you gather, analyse and calculate from a set of information to answer questions, and Sea Wolf, a simulation in which you choose the combination of options that best meets several criteria. Some longer invitations add a third, newer module. Older guides describe an ecosystem-building game that candidates report was phased out in 2025, so check the date on anything you read.

BCG Casey

BCG's online case is run by a chatbot called Casey. It walks you through one business case with a mix of multiple-choice and short written answers covering structuring, data and charts, and business maths. Candidates typically report around 8 to 10 questions in roughly half an hour, followed by a short recorded video in which you give your recommendation. Because the chatbot sets the order, it feels like an interviewer-led case. Where it sits in the process varies by office, so ask your recruiter.

The video is easy to underrate. Treat it like the end of a live case: answer first, two or three reasons with numbers, a risk and a next step. Practise with the 60-second recommendation.

Aptitude tests and other formats

Bain and several other firms use timed aptitude tests in some offices; the provider and the mix of numerical, verbal and logical questions vary. Some firms ask for recorded video answers instead of a first-round call. Whatever the format, read the instructions in your invitation closely: the duration, whether a calculator or scrap paper is allowed, whether you can go back to earlier questions, and whether there is a practice version.

How to prepare

  • Start with the invitation. A third-party article describing a named game is not evidence that you will get that game. Your invitation and the firm's own instructions are.
  • Do the official practice first. If the firm provides a demo or practice environment, do it. It removes most of the surprise.
  • Practise chart reading and business maths. These appear in almost every format. Use the chart drill and these maths questions.
  • Practise under time pressure. Pacing matters as much as accuracy.
  • Read the question before the data. Knowing what you are looking for stops you drowning in exhibits.
  • Follow the rules. If outside help or tools are not allowed, do not use them. Chasing leaked answers or screenshots is both against the rules and a poor use of time, because the content changes.

A worked example of the core skill

Most online tasks boil down to picking the relevant numbers and combining them correctly. Suppose a question says a product earns $12 of contribution per sale, a new sales channel would bring 4,000 extra sales a year, and the channel costs $15,000 a year to run. Should the client add it?

Extra contribution is 4,000 × $12 = $48,000. Subtract the $15,000 fixed cost and the channel adds $33,000 of profit a year, so yes. A distractor might give you the product's full price or last year's total sales; neither matters here. Spotting what to ignore is half the test.

On the day

  • Find a quiet room, a reliable connection and a charged laptop. Close other tabs and notifications.
  • Have paper, pens and, if allowed, a calculator ready.
  • Watch the clock. If the format lets you skip and return, do not get stuck on one question.
  • For any video part, check your camera, light and sound beforehand.

Check yourself

1. A guide from 2023 describes three McKinsey games. What do you do?

Show the answer

Treat it as history. Check your invitation and McKinsey's own instructions, and prepare the shared skills: reading data, calculating and choosing under several criteria.

2. A channel adds 2,400 sales a year at $0.30 contribution each but costs $1,000 a year. Worth it?

Show the answer

2,400 × $0.30 = $720 of contribution, less $1,000 of cost, is a $280 loss a year. No, unless it brings other benefits.

3. What should your recorded Casey recommendation contain?

Show the answer

The answer first, two or three reasons with numbers from the case, the main risk and a next step, in about a minute.

Keep it in proportion

Online tests are a gate, not the main event. Prepare enough to pass comfortably, then put most of your energy into live cases and fit stories. Start with how case interviews work and the guide to preparing from scratch.
